claim: One in ten women in their reproductive age suffer from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
source: One in ten women in their reproductive age suffer from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) that, alongside subfertility and hyperandrogenism, typically presents with increased luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility.
evidence: This is a statement about PCOS prevalence that draws from established medical knowledge.

claim: PCOS typically presents with increased luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility alongside subfertility and hyperandrogenism.
source: One in ten women in their reproductive age suffer from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) that, alongside subfertility and hyperandrogenism, typically presents with increased luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical features of PCOS based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Arcuate kisspeptin (ARNKISS) neurons represent the GnRH pulse generator and are suspected to be dysfunctional in PCOS.
source: As such, it is suspected that the arcuate kisspeptin (ARNKISS) neurons that represent the GnRH pulse generator are dysfunctional in PCOS.
evidence: This statement combines established knowledge about ARNKISS neurons with speculation about their role in PCOS.

claim: The peripubertal androgen (PPA) mouse model of PCOS had a reduction in the frequency of ARNKISS neuron synchronization events (SEs) that drive LH pulses.
source: We began with the peripubertal androgen (PPA) mouse model of PCOS but found that it had a reduction in the frequency of ARNKISS neuron synchronization events (SEs) that drive LH pulses.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The prenatal androgen (PNA) model of PCOS exhibited highly variable patterns of pulse generator activity.
source: Examining the prenatal androgen (PNA) model of PCOS, we observed highly variable patterns of pulse generator activity with no significant differences detected in ARNKISS neuron SEs, pulsatile LH secretion, or serum testosterone, estradiol, and progesterone concentrations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: No significant differences were detected in ARNKISS neuron SEs, pulsatile LH secretion, or serum testosterone, estradiol, and progesterone concentrations in the PNA model.
source: Examining the prenatal androgen (PNA) model of PCOS, we observed highly variable patterns of pulse generator activity with no significant differences detected in ARNKISS neuron SEs, pulsatile LH secretion, or serum testosterone, estradiol, and progesterone concentrations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A machine learning approach identified that the ARNKISS neurons of acyclic PNA mice continued to exhibit cyclical patterns of activity similar to that of normal mice.
source: However, a machine learning approach identified that the ARNKISS neurons of acyclic PNA mice continued to exhibit cyclical patterns of activity similar to that of normal mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data using machine learning analysis.

claim: The frequency of ARNKISS neuron SEs was significantly increased in algorithm-identified 'diestrous stage' PNA mice compared to controls.
source: The frequency of ARNKISS neuron SEs was significantly increased in algorithm-identified 'diestrous stage' PNA mice compared to controls.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: ARNKISS neurons exhibited reduced feedback suppression to progesterone in PNA mice.
source: In addition, ARNKISS neurons exhibited reduced feedback suppression to progesterone in PNA mice and their gonadotrophs were also less sensitive to GnRH.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Gonadotrophs in PNA mice were less sensitive to GnRH.
source: In addition, ARNKISS neurons exhibited reduced feedback suppression to progesterone in PNA mice and their gonadotrophs were also less sensitive to GnRH.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The existence of cyclical GnRH pulse generator activity in the acyclic PNA mouse indicates the presence of a complex phenotype with deficits at multiple levels of the hypothalamo-pituitary-gonadal axis.
source: The existence of cyclical GnRH pulse generator activity in the acyclic PNA mouse indicates the presence of a complex phenotype with deficits at multiple levels of the hypothalamo-pituitary-gonadal axis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: PCOS has variable reproductive and metabolic phenotypes.
source: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most common causes of female infertility with variable reproductive and metabolic phenotypes (Bozdag et al., 2016; Lizneva et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Up to 30% of PCOS patients do not have an elevated body mass index.
source: Many women with PCOS have an elevated body mass index but up to 30% of patients do not, resulting in PCOS being further classified into obese and lean subtypes (Nestler, 1997; Kumari et al., 2005; Toosy et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PCOS is classified into obese and lean subtypes.
source: Many women with PCOS have an elevated body mass index but up to 30% of patients do not, resulting in PCOS being further classified into obese and lean subtypes (Nestler, 1997; Kumari et al., 2005; Toosy et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Androgen excess, oligo-menorrhea/anovulation, and the existence of polycystic-like ovarian morphology are the key diagnostic indicators for PCOS.
source: Although androgen excess, oligo-menorrhea/anovulation, and the existence of polycystic-like ovarian morphology are the key diagnostic indicators for PCOS, a common secondary feature is increased luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility (Waldstreicher et al., 1988, Rotterdam ESHRE/ASRM-Sponsored PCOS consensus workshop group, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Increased luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility is a common secondary feature of PCOS.
source: Although androgen excess, oligo-menorrhea/anovulation, and the existence of polycystic-like ovarian morphology are the key diagnostic indicators for PCOS, a common secondary feature is increased luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility (Waldstreicher et al., 1988, Rotterdam ESHRE/ASRM-Sponsored PCOS consensus workshop group, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Basal and pulsatile LH secretion can be up to threefold higher in both lean and obese PCOS women.
source: Basal and pulsatile LH secretion can be up to threefold higher in both lean and obese PCOS women and are considered to be a significant contributor to their subfertility (Morales et al., 1996, Van Dam et al., 2002; Phylactou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Elevated LH secretion is considered to be a significant contributor to subfertility in PCOS women.
source: Basal and pulsatile LH secretion can be up to threefold higher in both lean and obese PCOS women and are considered to be a significant contributor to their subfertility (Morales et al., 1996, Van Dam et al., 2002; Phylactou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A presumed increase in the frequency of pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion in PCOS women results in an increased LH/follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) ratio.
source: A presumed increase in the frequency of pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion in PCOS women results in an increased LH/follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) ratio (Wildt et al., 1981; Dalkin et al., 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Increased LH/FSH ratio is thought to drive excess ovarian androgen production that impairs estrogen and progesterone feedback regulation of GnRH secretion.
source: This is thought to drive excess ovarian androgen production that, in turn, impairs estrogen and progesterone feedback regulation of GnRH secretion (Pastor et al., 1998; Chhabra et al., 2005; Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The arcuate nucleus kisspeptin (ARNKISS) neurons represent the mammalian GnRH pulse generator.
source: It has become clear that the arcuate nucleus kisspeptin (ARNKISS) neurons represent the mammalian GnRH pulse generator (Clarkson et al., 2017; Herbison, 2018; Goodman et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ARNKISS neurons exhibit brief episodes of synchronized activity that release kisspeptin on the distal projections of GnRH neurons to drive pulsatile GnRH secretion into the portal vasculature.
source: These neurons exhibit brief episodes of synchronized activity that release kisspeptin on the distal projections of GnRH neurons to drive pulsatile GnRH secretion into the portal vasculature (Herbison, 2021; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The synchronized activity amongst ARNKISS neurons required for pulsatile hormone secretion is generated by local glutamatergic transmission that is subsequently modulated by neurokinin B and dynorphin.
source: Recent studies indicate that the synchronized activity amongst ARNKISS neurons required for pulsatile hormone secretion is generated by local glutamatergic transmission that is subsequently modulated by neurokinin B and dynorphin (Qiu et al., 2016; Han et al., 2023; Morris and Herbison, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ARNKISS neurons are the primary site of estrogen negative feedback suppressing pulsatile GnRH secretion.
source: While the ARNKISS neurons are the primary site of estrogen negative feedback suppressing pulsatile GnRH secretion (McQuillan et al., 2022), the mechanism of progesterone feedback remains unclear but could also involve the ARNKISS neurons (Goodman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism of progesterone feedback remains unclear but could involve the ARNKISS neurons.
source: While the ARNKISS neurons are the primary site of estrogen negative feedback suppressing pulsatile GnRH secretion (McQuillan et al., 2022), the mechanism of progesterone feedback remains unclear but could also involve the ARNKISS neurons (Goodman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and involves speculation.

claim: Dysfunction within the ARNKISS neuron pulse generator may be responsible for the elevated LH pulse frequency observed in PCOS.
source: As such, it is thought that dysfunction within the ARNKISS neuron pulse generator may be responsible for the elevated LH pulse frequency observed in PCOS (Walters et al., 2018; Coutinho and Kauffman, 2019; Rodriguez Paris and Bertoldo, 2019; Ruddenklau and Campbell, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and involves speculation.

claim: PPA animals started to show a significant increase in weight 4 weeks after DHT capsule implantation compared to controls.
source: Female 129S6Sv/Ev C57BL/6 Kiss1Cre/+,GCaMP6s mice exposed to DHT from 3 weeks of age (PPA: n=4) started to show a significant increase in weight 4 weeks after capsule implantation compared to controls with empty capsules (control: n=5; Sidak's multiple comparisons test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PPA animals were completely acyclic with vaginal cytology only ever showing the diestrous stage.
source: The PPA animals were completely acyclic with vaginal cytology only ever showing the diestrous stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The frequency of SEs in PPA mice was approximately half that of controls.
source: The frequency of SEs in PPA mice (n=4) was approximately half that of controls (n=5) with SE frequency/hour showing an inhibitory trend (p=0.0714, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1C) and SE interval significantly increased (p=0.0159, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: SE interval was significantly increased in PPA mice compared to controls.
source: The frequency of SEs in PPA mice (n=4) was approximately half that of controls (n=5) with SE frequency/hour showing an inhibitory trend (p=0.0714, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1C) and SE interval significantly increased (p=0.0159, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SE duration, upswing and downswing durations were not significantly different between control and PPA animals.
source: These profiles were the same between control (n=5) and PPA (n=4) animals with SE duration, and both upswing and downswing durations, calculated from the full-width half maximum (FWHM) points, being not significantly different (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: PNA mice had a significantly increased anogenital distance compared with controls.
source: Female mice originating from dams treated with DHT on gestational days 16, 17, and 18 were found to have a significantly increased anogenital distance (n=10; p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U test) compared with controls (n=9; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Body weight was not different between PNA and control animals at 10 weeks of age.
source: Body weight was not different between PNA and control animals at 10 weeks of age (n=12 per group; p=0.6602, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PNA mice exhibited very disordered estrous cycles remaining mostly in persistent diestrus (71 ± 3%) with occasional excursions to metestrus.
source: The PNA mice exhibited very disordered estrous cycles remaining mostly in persistent diestrus (71 ± 3%) with occasional excursions to metestrus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The proestrous stage was never encountered and estrus was observed rarely in PNA mice.
source: The proestrous stage was never encountered and estrus was observed rarely (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Serum testosterone levels measured by ELISA did not differ between control and PNA animals in diestrus.
source: This did not detect any difference in serum testosterone levels between control (n=13) and PNA (n=20) animals in diestrus (p=0.8203, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No significant differences were detected for androstenedione, estradiol, or progesterone measured by LC-MS in diestrous PNA and control mice.
source: No significant differences (Mann-Whitney U tests) were detected for androstenedione, estradiol, or progesterone while all samples were below the limit of detection for testosterone (<0.01 ng/mL) (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: All samples were below the limit of detection for testosterone (<0.01 ng/mL) when measured by LC-MS.
source: No significant differences (Mann-Whitney U tests) were detected for androstenedione, estradiol, or progesterone while all samples were below the limit of detection for testosterone (<0.01 ng/mL) (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: PNA mice exhibited a significant but modest elevation in kisspeptin immunofluorescence within the rostral ARN.
source: This revealed a significant but modest elevation in kisspeptin immunofluorescence within the rostral ARN (p=0.0187, Sidak's multiple comparisons test) in PNA mice but not elsewhere in the ARN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant changes were detected for NKB or dynorphin immunoreactivity in any region of the ARN in PNA mice.
source: No significant changes were detected for NKB or dynorphin immunoreactivity in any region of the ARN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Overall SE frequency and intervals were not different between PNA and control animals.
source: However, overall SE frequency and intervals were not different between PNA (n=6) and control (n=7) animals (Figure 3E and F; Mann-Whitney U tests).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Continuous (10 Hz) photometry recordings in diestrus did not reveal any difference in the profiles of single SEs between controls and PNA animals.
source: Continuous (10 Hz) photometry recordings in diestrus did not reveal any difference in the profiles of single SEs between controls (n=7) and PNA (n=6) animals (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: Every SE was followed by an LH pulse, and no LH pulses were detected without a preceding SE in both control and PNA mice.
source: We observed a perfect correlation between SEs and pulsatile LH secretions in both control and PNA mice: every SE was followed by an LH pulse, and no LH pulses were detected without a preceding SE (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: The SE peak precedes each LH peak by 7.7±0.6 min in control mice and 6.6±0.4 min in PNA mice.
source: Temporal analysis of SEs and LH release indicated that the SE peak precedes each LH peak by 7.7±0.6 min and 6.6±0.4 min in control (n=7 from 4 mice) and PNA (n=7 from 5 mice) animals (p=0.190, Mann-Whitney U test), respectively (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Mean LH levels were found to be significantly elevated in PNA mice compared to controls.
source: Mean LH levels were found to be significantly elevated in PNA mice (p=0.0205, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 4E–G) but the variable LH pulse frequency (p=0.1843, Mann-Whitney U test) and amplitude (p=0.4630, Mann-Whitney U test) were unchanged compared to controls (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: LH pulse frequency and amplitude were unchanged in PNA mice compared to controls.
source: Mean LH levels were found to be significantly elevated in PNA mice (p=0.0205, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 4E–G) but the variable LH pulse frequency (p=0.1843, Mann-Whitney U test) and amplitude (p=0.4630, Mann-Whitney U test) were unchanged compared to controls (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H, I.

claim: PNA mice showed a small but significantly lower level of LH 20 min after GnRH injection compared to controls.
source: However, PNA mice showed a small but significantly lower level of LH 20 min after GnRH injection (p=0.0152, Sidak's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The total GnRH-evoked increment in LH release was significantly lower in PNA mice compared to controls.
source: The total GnRH-evoked increment in LH release was significantly lower in PNA mice compared to controls (p=0.0028, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 4K).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The proportion of Cluster_0 and Cluster_1 activity was almost identical between control and PNA mice over four days.
source: The proportion of Cluster_0 (PNA 21%; control 21%) and Cluster_1 (PNA 44%; control 42%) activity was almost identical with the major trend being a nonsignificant increased time (p>0.05, Sidak's multiple comparisons test) spent in mpSE Cluster_3/4 activity (PNA 20%; control 12%) at the expense of the fast regular SE Cluster_2 pattern (PNA 15%; control 25%; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The frequency of SEs was 48% greater in algorithm-identified 'diestrous-like' PNA mice compared to control animals.
source: In this case, the frequency of SEs was 48% greater in PNA mice (n=6) compared to control animals (n=7; p=0.0029, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 6C) and was also reflected in a significantly lower inter-SE interval (p=0.0047, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Inter-SE interval was significantly lower in algorithm-identified 'diestrous-like' PNA mice compared to controls.
source: In this case, the frequency of SEs was 48% greater in PNA mice (n=6) compared to control animals (n=7; p=0.0029, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 6C) and was also reflected in a significantly lower inter-SE interval (p=0.0047, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Progesterone caused a marked suppression of ARNKISS neuron SEs that lasted for up to 6 hr in control mice.
source: As expected (McQuillan et al., 2019), we found a marked suppression of ARNKISS neuron SEs (n=3, progesterone main effect F(1,10)=7.333, p=0.022) that lasted for up to 6 hr following progesterone in control mice (n=3, p<0.001, Sidak's multiple comparisons test, Figure 7A, B and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A, B and E.

claim: The response to progesterone in PNA mice was much less consistent, and overall, no significant differences in SE activity were detected at any time point.
source: The response in PNA mice was much less consistent, and overall, no significant differences in SE activity detected at any time point (n=3, progesterone main effect, F(1,10)=1.917, p=0.196, Figure 7C, D and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C, D and F.

claim: No significant differences exist between SE frequency or intervals in ovariectomized PNA and control animals.
source: We observed no significant differences (Mann-Whitney U tests) between SE frequency (Figure 8C) or intervals (Figure 8D and E) in PNA and control animals (n=4 per group).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C, D and E.

claim: High-resolution recordings at 10 Hz did not reveal any differences in SE profiles between OVX control and OVX PNA mice.
source: Similarly, high-resolution recordings at 10 Hz did not reveal any differences in SE profiles between OVX control and OVX PNA mice (Figure 8F and H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and H.

claim: The PPA mouse model does not provide an appropriate PCOS model of elevated pulse generator activity.
source: This clearly indicates that the PPA mouse does not provide an appropriate PCOS model of elevated pulse generator activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Chronic excess androgen activation in the PPA model likely provides additional negative feedback suppression of ARNKISS neurons.
source: It is very likely that chronic excess androgen activation in this model provides additional negative feedback suppression of ARNKISS neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Treatment of adult OVX female mice with DHT is reported to decrease LH pulse frequency and amplitude.
source: The treatment of adult OVX female mice with the same DHT regimen is reported to decrease LH pulse frequency and amplitude (Esparza et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Increased anogenital distance, normal body weight, and highly disrupted estrous cycles are common characteristics of the PNA mouse model.
source: Common characteristics, also present in the current study, are those of increased anogenital distance, normal body weight, and highly disrupted estrous cycles (Sullivan and Moenter, 2004; Silva et al., 2018; Stener-Victorin et al., 2020; Gibson et al., 2021; McCarthy et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: Reported differences in circulating gonadal steroid concentrations in PNA mice have been highly inconsistent among studies.
source: In contrast, reported differences in circulating gonadal steroid concentrations in PNA mice have been highly inconsistent among studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature that draws from knowledge of prior studies.

claim: Some studies have demonstrated PNA mice to have elevated testosterone levels while others find no differences.
source: Using ELISAs and radioimmunoassyays, some studies have demonstrated PNA mice to have elevated testosterone levels while others, including ourselves, find no differences (Sullivan and Moenter, 2004; Roland et al., 2010; Roland and Moenter, 2011; Moore et al., 2015; Lei et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and data from the current study.

claim: Concerns exist over the specificity and selectivity of ELISAs for measuring gonadal steroids in mice.
source: Concerns over the specificity and selectivity of ELISAs for measuring gonadal steroids in mice (Handelsman and Wartofsky, 2013; Auchus, 2014; Wierman et al., 2014; Handelsman et al., 2015) led us to re-assess gonadal steroid hormone levels using gold-standard ultrasensitive LC-MS (Handelsman et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It remains unclear if and when testosterone levels are elevated in PNA mice.
source: Unfortunately, this was not the case, and overall it remains unclear if and when testosterone levels are elevated in PNA mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings and literature.

claim: A prior ELISA assessment reported that estradiol and progesterone levels were unchanged in PNA animals.
source: A prior ELISA assessment also reported that estradiol and progesterone levels were unchanged in PNA animals (Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There is considerable inconsistency among studies regarding the effects of PNA treatment on mRNA and protein expression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin in the ARN.
source: Another area of considerable inconsistency among studies involves the effects of PNA treatment on both mRNA and protein expression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin in the ARN (Yan et al., 2014; Osuka et al., 2016; Gibson et al., 2021; McCarthy et al., 2022; Moore et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Any PNA-induced changes in the expression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin are subtle.
source: While there are important roles for these neuropeptides in modulating ARNKISS neuron synchronizations (Han et al., 2023; Morris and Herbison, 2023) and their subsequent activation of GnRH secretion (Liu et al., 2021), these generally inconsistent findings indicate that any PNA-induced changes in the expression of the neuropeptides are subtle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings and literature.

claim: The principal determinant of kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin expression in ARNKISS neurons is estradiol.
source: Indeed, the principal determinant of kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin expression in ARNKISS neurons is estradiol (Navarro et al., 2009) and we demonstrate here that circulating estradiol levels are not altered in PNA mice.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and data from the current study.

claim: Increased pulsatile LH secretion is thought to be a key feature of the PNA mouse model.
source: One of the key features of the PNA mouse model is thought to be that of increased pulsatile LH secretion (Stener-Victorin et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Only one study has reported that PNA mice exhibit an approximately 40% increase in LH pulse frequency.
source: However, this has only been reported in a single study with PNA mice exhibiting an approximately 40% increase in LH pulse frequency (Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A recent paper found that LH pulse frequency was not significantly altered in PNA mice.
source: A recent paper undertaking the same tail-tip pulse bleeding approach found that LH pulse frequency was not significantly altered in PNA mice (McCarthy et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: It is essentially impossible to define the 'pulse generator stage' of a PNA mouse at the time of bleeding because the pulse generator continues to cycle in the acyclic PNA mouse.
source: As the pulse generator continues to cycle in the acyclic PNA mouse, it is essentially impossible to define the 'pulse generator stage' of a PNA mouse at the time of bleeding and consequently wide variations in LH pulse frequency would be expected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The PNA mouse model may to some degree replicate the increased pulse frequency seen in many women with PCOS.
source: As such, the PNA mouse model may to some degree replicate the increased pulse frequency seen in many women with PCOS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The dynamics of individual ARNKISS neuron SEs remain unchanged under all conditions in PNA mice.
source: We also note that the dynamics of individual ARNKISS neuron SEs remain unchanged under all conditions in PNA mice, suggesting that the fundamental synchronization mechanism and numbers of contributing neurons is not altered (Han et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings supported by a citation.

claim: PNA treatment does not alter ARNKISS neuron firing activity in adult acute brain slices.
source: This is consistent with the observation that PNA treatment does not alter ARNKISS neuron firing activity in adult acute brain slices (Gibson et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The acyclic reproductive phenotype of PNA mice does not result from an absence of cyclical activity in the pulse generator.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the acyclic reproductive phenotype of PNA mice does not result from an absence of cyclical activity in the pulse generator.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Pulse generation in the mouse does not depend on action potential generation by GnRH neurons.
source: Although pulse generation in the mouse does not depend on action potential generation by GnRH neurons (Wang et al., 2020; Herbison, 2021), it is noteworthy that a significant impact of PNA treatment on the activity of the GnRH neuron can be excluded (Jaime and Moenter, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A significant impact of PNA treatment on the activity of the GnRH neuron can be excluded.
source: Although pulse generation in the mouse does not depend on action potential generation by GnRH neurons (Wang et al., 2020; Herbison, 2021), it is noteworthy that a significant impact of PNA treatment on the activity of the GnRH neuron can be excluded (Jaime and Moenter, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A very wide range of LH pulse frequency is found in anovulatory women with PCOS.
source: However, a very wide range of LH pulse frequency is found in anovulatory women with PCOS (Taylor et al., 1997), suggesting the intriguing possibility that the GnRH pulse generator activity may also continue to cycle in women with PCOS.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The GnRH pulse generator activity may continue to cycle in women with PCOS.
source: However, a very wide range of LH pulse frequency is found in anovulatory women with PCOS (Taylor et al., 1997), suggesting the intriguing possibility that the GnRH pulse generator activity may also continue to cycle in women with PCOS.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and literature.

claim: Pulse generator activity was found to be identical in ovariectomized PNA and control mice.
source: Pulse generator activity was found to be identical in ovariectomized PNA and control mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Perinatal DHT exposure does not engender any fundamental differences in ARNKISS neuron synchronization behavior in the absence of gonads as adults.
source: This indicates that, despite androgen receptors being expressed by ARNKISS neurons in the perinatal period (Watanabe et al., 2023), excess DHT exposure at this time does not engender any fundamental differences in their synchronization behavior in the absence of gonads as adults.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings supported by a citation.

claim: The subtle increase in pulse generator frequency detected in 'diestrous-like' PNA mice arises from the effects of circulating gonadal steroids.
